chapters.title: Chapter 5: Behavioral Economics in Organizations and the Workplace

lessons.title: Sunk Cost Fallacy in Corporate Decision-Making: Why Bad Projects Don't Die

children.text: A company has spent ₹12 crore building a software platform. Early customer feedback is lukewarm, a competitor just launched something better, and finishing the last stretch will cost another ₹4 crore. In the boardroom, someone says what everyone is already thinking: "We can't stop now, we've already put in twelve crore." It sounds like caution. It is actually the single most well-documented reasoning error in corporate decision-making, and this lesson explains exactly why it feels so persuasive while being completely irrelevant to the decision at hand.

body.text: A sunk cost is money, time, or effort already spent that cannot be recovered no matter what happens next. Rational decision-making says a sunk cost should have zero influence on a forward-looking choice, only the future costs and benefits from this point on matter. Almost nobody actually decides this way, and organizations are often worse at it than individuals.

children.text: The Sunk Cost Fallacy: Why the Past Shouldn't Matter

markDefs.definition: The tendency to let past, unrecoverable costs influence a present decision, even though rational choice theory says only future costs and benefits from this point forward should matter.

children.text: Psychologists Hal Arkes and Catherine Blumer established the

as a robust, repeatable pattern in a 1985 paper, showing across several experiments that people who had already paid for something were more likely to keep using it, even when a free or better alternative existed, purely because of the earlier, unrecoverable payment. The ₹12 crore already spent on the software platform is gone whether the company finishes it or cancels it today. The only number that should matter is whether the remaining ₹4 crore in future spending is worth what the finished product will actually earn. Everything already spent is, economically, a rounding error on a decision that hasn't been made yet.

body.title: Do the forward-looking maths
body.prompt: Ignoring the ₹12 crore already spent, completing the platform costs ₹4 crore more and is expected to generate ₹9 crore in additional revenue once launched. What is the correct forward-looking net benefit of completing the project, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: ₹9 crore expected revenue − ₹4 crore remaining cost = ₹5 crore net benefit. The ₹12 crore already spent doesn't appear anywhere in this calculation, because it's unrecoverable regardless of what the company decides today. Note that this example happens to favor continuing, which is the point: ignoring sunk cost doesn't mean automatically killing every project with a large past spend, it means judging every project purely on what's left.

body.text: Now change one number: if the remaining cost were ₹10 crore against the same ₹9 crore expected revenue, the correct decision flips to stopping, regardless of whether ₹2 crore or ₹20 crore had already been spent. The sunk cost fallacy isn't really about optimism or pessimism. It's about letting an irrelevant number quietly sit inside a calculation where it has no business being.

children.text: Escalation of Commitment: The Organizational Version

markDefs.definition: Barry Staw's term for the tendency to increase commitment to a failing course of action, especially when the decision-maker personally made the original choice, driven partly by a need to justify that earlier decision rather than by the sunk cost alone.

children.text: Organizational behavior researcher Barry Staw sharpened this picture in a 1976 study he titled "Knee-Deep in the Big Muddy," borrowing the phrase from a protest folk song about a commander pushing troops further into a river despite mounting evidence it was a mistake. Staw gave participants a simulated business investment decision, and the critical variable wasn't the size of the past investment, it was who had made the original choice. Participants who had personally made the initial investment decision allocated significantly more additional funding to a subsequently failing division than participants who were simply handed the same failing situation to evaluate fresh. Staw called this

: the sunk cost fallacy, plus a second, separate force, the psychological need to justify having made the original decision at all. Admitting the project should stop isn't just accepting a financial loss. For the person who championed it, it can feel like admitting they were wrong in the first place, a distinct cost the pure financial sunk cost fallacy doesn't capture.

body.caption: Two related but distinct forces keeping a bad project alive

cells: Letting past, unrecoverable spending influence a forward-looking decision
Anyone evaluating the project, regardless of their role in starting it
Self-justification: needing the original decision to have been right
Specifically the person or team who made the original decision

children.text: Why Organizations Are Often Worse at This Than Individuals

A person deciding whether to finish a bad meal only has their own stubbornness to overcome. A company deciding whether to kill a bad project has several amplifiers stacked on top of ordinary sunk cost thinking. The person recommending cancellation is often not the person who championed the project, creating exactly the political dynamic Staw's study measured. Publicly cancelling a project can carry a direct, visible career cost for its sponsor in a way privately abandoning a personal hobby never does. And a team that has spent months building a shared narrative around a project's eventual success faces a version of the information cascade from Chapter 3: each person's continued confidence looks, to everyone else on the team, like independent evidence the project is worth continuing, when it may really just be everyone reading the same shared optimism back to each other. The next lesson in this chapter, on groupthink, picks up exactly this thread.
A Framework to Escape the Trap: Zero-Based Re-Evaluation

Staw's finding points directly at the most effective organizational fix: separate the person evaluating whether to continue from the person who made the original decision. Some private equity firms and venture capital investors formalize this as a deliberate governance practice, routing follow-on investment decisions above a certain size through a review that includes people who weren't part of the original approval, specifically to short-circuit escalation of commitment rather than relying on the original team's willpower. Paired with a simple forward-looking test, asking only "given everything we know now, and treating all past spending as zero, would we choose to invest going forward from here," this converts an emotionally loaded question about admitting failure into a clean, mechanical calculation, exactly the ₹4 crore versus ₹9 crore comparison from earlier in this lesson.

body.title: Who should make the call?
body.scenario: A retail chain's Head of E-commerce personally championed a ₹20 crore investment in a new delivery app three years ago. Growth has consistently missed targets, and a rival platform now dominates the segment. The Head of E-commerce is presenting a proposal for another ₹6 crore to "finally fix" the app's core issues, projecting it will unlock ₹5 crore in additional annual revenue.
body.prompt: Using what you've learned about escalation of commitment, how should the company structure this decision?
body.modelAnswer:
1. The Head of E-commerce is the worst-positioned person to give a fully objective recommendation here, not because they're dishonest, but because Staw's research shows the original decision-maker specifically tends to over-commit to justify the earlier choice.
2. The ₹20 crore already spent should play no role in whether the additional ₹6 crore is worth spending. The only relevant comparison is the ₹6 crore future cost against realistic future returns, evaluated independently of who is presenting the case.
3. The projected ₹5 crore in additional annual revenue against a ₹6 crore cost is worth real scrutiny on its own assumptions, ideally reviewed by someone outside the original team, given the proposal is coming from the person with the strongest self-justification incentive to make the numbers look favorable.
4. A sound process would route this decision through leadership who didn't approve the original ₹20 crore, explicitly frame the question as a fresh investment decision rather than a continuation, and require the same rigor, and the same right to say no, that a genuinely new ₹6 crore proposal from any other team would receive.

body.title: Sunk cost fallacy, or escalation of commitment?
body.question: Two managers separately review the same failing project and recommend continuing it. Manager A originally approved the project two years ago. Manager B is reviewing it for the first time this week, after being handed the file cold, and still recommends continuing, citing only the amount already invested. Whose reasoning is a purer example of the plain sunk cost fallacy, distinct from escalation of commitment?
options: Manager A, because they have the strongest self-justification motive
Manager B, because their reasoning cites only the unrecoverable past spending, with no personal responsibility for the original decision at play
Both equally, since escalation of commitment and the sunk cost fallacy are exactly the same thing
Neither, since citing the amount already invested is actually a valid forward-looking consideration
body.explanation: Manager B's reasoning is the plain sunk cost fallacy in isolation: no personal stake in having made the original call, just the past-spending logic Arkes and Blumer described. Manager A's identical recommendation is more likely escalation of commitment, since Staw's research found the original decision-maker's self-justification need adds a second force on top of the sunk cost fallacy itself.

body.title: Name Staw's term
body.textWithBlank: Barry Staw's term for increasing commitment to a failing course of action, especially by the person who made the original decision, is ___ of commitment.
body.explanation: Escalation of commitment adds self-justification, the need to have been right about the original decision, on top of the plain sunk cost fallacy, which is why it hits the original decision-maker specifically harder than a neutral evaluator.

body.title: Where does the term "Concorde fallacy" come from?

children.text: The sunk cost fallacy is sometimes called the Concorde fallacy, or Concorde effect, after the British and French governments' supersonic passenger jet programme, which continued for years after it had become clear the aircraft would never be commercially profitable. The name has become a common shorthand across psychology and economics for exactly the dynamic this lesson covers: a large past investment continuing to justify further investment, in a joint government programme, a corporate software platform, or a personal ski-trip ticket in Arkes and Blumer's original experiments, regardless of the actual scale involved.

body.label: What determined who escalated, in Staw's study
body.context: Not the size of the past investment. Participants who had personally chosen the original course of action allocated significantly more additional funding to a failing project than those evaluating it fresh.

cards.definition: Letting past, unrecoverable spending influence a present decision, even though rational choice theory says only future costs and benefits should matter.
Barry Staw's term for increasing commitment to a failing course of action, driven partly by the original decision-maker's need to justify that earlier choice.
A common alternate name for the sunk cost fallacy, referencing the British-French supersonic jet programme that continued despite clear evidence of commercial non-viability.
Evaluating a project purely on its remaining future costs and benefits, treating all past spending as irrelevant, as if deciding fresh today.
A decision-maker without personal responsibility for a project's original approval, used deliberately in some governance structures to short-circuit escalation of commitment.

points: A sunk cost is unrecoverable no matter what happens next, and rational decision-making says it should have zero weight in a forward-looking choice, only the remaining future costs and benefits matter.
Ignoring sunk costs doesn't mean automatically killing every expensive project. It means judging every project purely on what's left to spend against what it's still expected to return.

Barry Staw's research found escalation of commitment is driven specifically by who made the original decision, not by the size of the past investment, adding a self-justification force on top of the plain sunk cost fallacy.

Organizations amplify individual sunk cost bias through career risk for the original sponsor, and through the same information-cascade dynamic from Chapter 3 playing out inside a team's shared confidence in its own project.

The practical fix is structural, not willpower: separate the person evaluating whether to continue from the person who made the original call, and frame the decision as a fresh, zero-based investment choice rather than a continuation.
